Title: Department of Transportation - Human Trafficking Awareness, Training, and Response (See Someone, Save Someone Act)
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 437

NarrowSubjects.Name: Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc

bill_summary: This bill, known as the See Someone, Save Someone Act, requires the Maryland Department of Transportation (MDOT) to develop and implement a training program for certain transportation sector employees and contractors on the identification and reporting of suspected human trafficking. Employers must certify annually that their employees have completed this training, establish reporting procedures, and implement a human trafficking prevention policy. Additionally, MDOT is required to provide public service announcements in both English and Spanish regarding safety information for trafficking victims at airports, transit stations, ports, and highway rest stops.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation
stakeholders: State and contract employees at transit stations, airports, port facilities, and highway rest stops; transit service providers; transportation sector employers; and potential human trafficking victims.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures from the Transportation Trust Fund increase by an estimated $262,500 in FY 2026 and $137,500 in FY 2027 to develop the training curriculum and cover overtime costs for employee attendance. No impact on State revenues or local government finances is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency named in the bill, MDOT is responsible for developing, identifying, and implementing the human trafficking training program and ensuring the execution of public service announcements at transportation facilities.

MTA is specifically impacted as the bill mandates training for employees at transit stations and those providing transit services. The fiscal note also indicates MTA will likely lead the development of the training curriculum.
SHA is responsible for managing highway rest stops, where the bill mandates both employee training and the provision of human trafficking safety public service announcements.
MAA operates BWI and Martin State airports, both of which are specific locations where employees must be trained and public service announcements must be implemented.
MPA manages port facilities, which are designated locations requiring staff training and the implementation of public service announcements under the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP manages the Safe Harbor Regional Navigator Grant Program; the bill requires employers to establish procedures for reporting suspected trafficking to 'designated regional navigators,' which fall under GOCPP's administration.
MSP often provides security and law enforcement at MDOT facilities and highway rest stops; they would likely be the primary 'appropriate local agency' receiving reports of suspected trafficking.
The MDTA manages toll facilities and has its own police force that protects ports and airports; its personnel and facilities may be impacted by the training and reporting protocols.
DHS is involved in victim services and was identified as a stakeholder in the legislative analysis for the development of trafficking response protocols.
MDH collaborates on statewide human trafficking awareness and training initiatives and is a stakeholder in coordinating responses to potential victims.
DBM is responsible for the state's personnel and fiscal management; the bill has a notable fiscal impact on the Transportation Trust Fund for training and overtime costs.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MDOT and would be responsible for advising on the immunity provisions for employees reporting incidents in good faith.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch agencies (MDOT) and signs the legislation into law; it also plays a role in coordinating multi-agency anti-trafficking efforts.
As a modal unit of MDOT, the MVA is generally responsible for driver and vehicle safety, though the bill focuses more on stations and ports.
MSDE is mentioned in the fiscal note as having existing human trafficking training mandates, serving as a policy precedent and potential collaborator for curriculum development.
Morgan State University was listed as an information source for the fiscal note, indicating minimal impact or consultation regarding the bill's implementation.
Saint Mary's College was listed as an information source for the fiscal note, indicating minimal impact or consultation regarding the bill's implementation.
The University System of Maryland was listed as an information source for the fiscal note, indicating minimal impact or consultation regarding the bill's implementation.

Synopsis: Clarifying the definition of "physical therapist assistant" as used in the Maryland Physical Therapy Act to mean an individual licensed by the State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners; increasing the membership of the State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners from 8 to 9; and requiring the Board to send renewal notices to licensees by electronic means, rather than first-class mail, unless the licensee requests to receive the renewal notice by first-class mail.
Title: State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners - Revisions
Status: Approved by the Governor - Chapter 352

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits

bill_summary: This bill clarifies the definition of physical therapist assistant within the Maryland Physical Therapy Act and expands the State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners from eight to nine members by adding a second licensed physical therapist assistant. Additionally, the bill changes the default method for license renewal notifications from first-class mail to electronic means, unless a licensee specifically requests to receive the notice by mail.
responsible_party: State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners
stakeholders: Physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, and the State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners.
fiscal_impact_summary: Beginning in fiscal 2026, State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners special fund expenditures are expected to increase by $1,500 annually for the additional board member's compensation. However, the move to electronic renewal notices is expected to save approximately $5,000 annually in mailing costs, resulting in a net special fund expenditure savings of approximately $3,500 per year. There is no impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill has a direct fiscal impact on the State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners' special fund expenditures, including a $1,500 annual increase for member compensation and an estimated $5,000 annual decrease in mailing costs. As the state's central fiscal authority, DBM oversees budget formulation and the personnel systems related to these changes.

The State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners is a regulatory body operating under the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly alters the Board's membership, clarifies the definition of 'physical therapist assistant' in the Health Occupations Article, and mandates changes to the Board's administrative procedures for license renewals.

The Governor is the appointing authority for members of the State Board of Physical Therapy Examiners. The bill increases the number of Board members from 8 to 9 and explicitly requires the Governor to appoint the additional licensed physical therapist assistant member.

This office is responsible for identifying, recruiting, and vetting candidates to serve on Maryland's boards and commissions. It will manage the application and vetting process for the new board member position established by this legislation to ensure the candidate meets the specific professional requirements.

bill_summary: This bill establishes specific criteria for what constitutes an unreasonable restriction on the installation of solar collector systems by community associations, defining it as a restriction that increases the system's cost by at least 5% or reduces its energy generation by at least 10%. It also clarifies the authority of community associations to prohibit or set reasonable restrictions on solar installations in common areas and requires property owners to provide documentation from certified solar panel design specialists to prove a restriction is unreasonable.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and Community Associations (homeowners and condominium associations)
stakeholders: Maryland property owners, community associations, boards of directors of real estate developments, and solar panel design specialists.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially impact State or local government operations or finances. The impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal as described in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Energy Administration is the primary state agency responsible for renewable energy policy and initiatives. This bill directly impacts the adoption of solar collector systems by defining what constitutes an unreasonable restriction on their installation, a topic central to the MEA's mission of promoting clean energy and lowering costs for residents.

The bill explicitly mentions the Director of the Maryland Historical Trust, which is a division of the Department of Planning. The Trust is responsible for determining which properties are eligible for inclusion in the Maryland Register of Historic Properties, and the bill exempts such historic properties from the new solar installation rules.

The bill establishes specific legal thresholds (5% cost increase and 10% efficiency reduction) to determine if a restriction is 'unreasonable.' Disputes between property owners and community associations regarding these definitions will be adjudicated through the Maryland court system, which is supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The Maryland Clean Energy Center works to accelerate the adoption of clean energy and make sustainable technology more affordable. The bill's provisions to limit the financial and efficiency impacts of HOA restrictions directly align with the Center's work to reduce barriers for residents transitioning to solar energy.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and handles advocacy work regarding consumer protection and real property law. They may be involved in interpreting the impact of these changes on homeowners' rights and community association governance.

bill_summary: This bill updates the terminology and reporting requirements for the Maryland Food System Resiliency Council. It defines 'healthy food priority areas' and 'wasted food' to replace outdated terms like 'food deserts' and 'food waste,' and tasks the Council with developing equity and sustainability policy recommendations. Additionally, it repeals several outdated one-time reporting requirements while establishing a permanent requirement for an annual report on the Council's findings and recommended legislative changes.
responsible_party: Maryland Food System Resiliency Council within the Maryland Department of Emergency Management
stakeholders: Maryland residents experiencing food insecurity, local food council organizations, Maryland food businesses, schools, institutions of higher education, and nonprofit organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Emergency Management can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on State revenues, and the bill is not anticipated to materially affect local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Food System Resiliency Council is explicitly housed within the Office of Resilience at MDEM, and the Secretary of Emergency Management is the primary executive authority defined in the bill. MDEM also provides the staffing and administrative support for the Council.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Food System Resiliency Council functions as a specialized advisory body within the executive branch, which is the primary subject of this legislation.

The bill mandates that the Council make specific recommendations to the Maryland State Department of Education regarding the federal Community Eligibility Provision for student nutrition and targets local food procurement through schools.

The Council's goals include increasing the production, aggregation, marketing, and distribution of local food, as well as creating market opportunities for Maryland food businesses and expanding food production infrastructure.
The Council is tasked with addressing diet-related public health disparities and food insecurity, which are core components of the Department of Health’s public health and disease prevention mission.

The bill defines and targets 'wasted food' management, including composting and anaerobic digestion, and tasks the Council with addressing environmental impacts related to food waste, which aligns with MDE's regulatory and environmental protection oversight.

DHS is the primary provider of SNAP and other economic assistance; the Council’s goal to coordinate State and local level food insecurity services directly intersects with DHS's social service delivery.
The GOC leads a whole-of-government approach to child poverty and food insecurity, mirroring the Council's goals to coordinate statewide food services and address student nutrition.

The bill specifically directs the Council to increase local food aggregation and distribution in rural settings and expand access to food production infrastructure, which are central to RMC's mission of supporting rural economic development and infrastructure.
The bill explicitly tasks the Council with increasing the procurement of local food through 'institutions of higher education' and 'universities,' which directly impacts USM's procurement policies.
As a primary procurement unit and institution of higher education, Morgan State is directly impacted by the bill's goal to increase local food procurement at universities.
As a public institution of higher education, the college is a target for the Council's goals regarding increased local food procurement by state institutions.
MHEC coordinates policy for public and private colleges and universities; the bill's goal to increase local food procurement at these institutions may require MHEC's coordinating involvement.
The bill defines 'healthy food priority areas' and tasks the Council with mapping food insecurity, which utilizes demographic and land-use data analysis typically managed by MDP.

The Council's mission to create market opportunities for Maryland food businesses and increase marketing of local products aligns with the Department of Commerce’s role in economic development and business support.
The Governor oversees the executive departments housing the Council (MDEM) and signs the resulting reports and legislative proposals into law.

bill_summary: This bill permanently extends and expands requirements for health insurance carriers to provide referrals to out-of-network specialists when a suitable in-network provider is unavailable within specific travel and wait-time standards. It specifically focuses on mental health and substance use disorder (SUD) services, requiring carriers to assist members in arranging coverage and ensuring cost-sharing remains at in-network levels for the duration of a treatment plan. It also prohibits insurers from imposing stricter utilization reviews on these out-of-network referrals than they would for in-network providers.
responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration and Maryland Health Care Commission
stakeholders: Health insurance policyholders seeking mental health or substance use disorder treatment, health insurance carriers, and behavioral health providers
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no fiscal effect in FY 2025. In FY 2026, the Maryland Insurance Administration will see a minimal increase in special fund revenue from $125 rate and form filing fees. The bill is not expected to impact the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program or local government finances. Small business healthcare practices may see a meaningful impact as nonparticipating providers may serve more patients under the bill's referral provisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the state's insurance industry, the MIA is responsible for enforcing the insurance laws amended by this bill, which governs carrier referral procedures, utilization reviews, and reimbursement for nonparticipating providers.

The bill specifically mandates that the MHCC hold public meetings with stakeholders to determine a reimbursement formula for nonparticipating providers delivering mental health and substance use disorder services.

The bill focuses on access to mental health and substance use disorder services, which fall under the oversight of the MDH's behavioral health programs, and the MHCC is an independent unit within this department.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Health Care Commission regarding the implementation and enforcement of new health insurance regulations.
DBM is involved in the fiscal analysis of the bill to determine if the changes to insurance law would impact the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program.
The Governor's Office is responsible for signing the bill into law and oversees the executive agencies (MIA and MDH) charged with implementing these mental health access policies.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the sale and distribution of products containing tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) that violate Maryland's potency, packaging, or labeling requirements. It authorizes the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission (ATCC) to issue citations and seize or destroy illegal products, while establishing that displaying THC products for sale without a license is evidence of an illegal sale.
responsible_party: Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission (ATCC) and the Maryland Cannabis Administration (MCA)
stakeholders: Cannabis business licensees, unlicensed retailers of THC products, Maryland consumers, and law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues are expected to increase minimally starting in fiscal 2026 due to the collection of misdemeanor fines and citations. The bill is not expected to have a significant impact on state or local expenditures, as the ATCC and MCA can implement its provisions using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator for medical and adult-use cannabis in Maryland, the MCA is responsible for overseeing license compliance and taking disciplinary actions against licensees who violate the potency, packaging, or labeling requirements established by this bill.

The OCSA enforces the state's Controlled Dangerous Substances Act and monitors the legal supply chain. This bill regulates the sale of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) products, including delta-8 and delta-10, which fall under the OCSA's broader mission of preventing drug abuse and diversion.

The Department of Health oversees public health services and regulatory oversight of healthcare and controlled substances. As the parent agency of the OCSA, it is involved in the health-related impacts of regulating intoxicating cannabinoids.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor for the Maryland Cannabis Administration and other state agencies. It would be responsible for providing legal counsel on the enforcement of these new regulations and managing any subsequent criminal or civil appeals.

The bill establishes new misdemeanor offenses and authorizes the issuance of citations for non-licensees. The AOC manages the District Court system where these cases and civil citations will be adjudicated.

The bill grants enforcement powers to the Field Enforcement Division, whose officers are sworn police officers. The MSP investigates major crimes, including illegal drug distribution, and often works in coordination with other law enforcement units on statewide drug enforcement efforts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Because the bill creates new misdemeanor offenses for the sale of unauthorized THC products, the OPD would be responsible for providing legal representation to indigent residents charged under these provisions.

The Governor’s Office oversees all state departments and agencies, including the ATCC and MCA. The Governor signed this legislation and directs the statewide initiatives regarding public safety and economic opportunity affected by cannabis regulation.

The bill specifies that the Field Enforcement Division may work and cooperate with the Office of the Comptroller. Additionally, the division's enforcement duties include handling cannabis on which state taxes are due and unpaid.

The OAH conducts formal hearings for contested cases from state agencies. It may be required to adjudicate appeals from cannabis licensees facing disciplinary action by the MCA for potency or labeling violations.

The bill explicitly references the definition of 'hemp' from the Agriculture Article to differentiate it from other THC products, impacting how the MDA's regulatory oversight of hemp production interacts with cannabis enforcement.
The bill notes that the Field Enforcement Division may employ officers and employees as provided in the State budget, which is formulated and overseen by DBM.

The OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits of the MCA and ATCC to ensure that these agencies are following state laws and financial controls when enforcing the bill's provisions and managing confiscated products.

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Maryland Limited Worker Cooperative Association Act, which authorizes the formation, operation, governance, and dissolution of limited worker cooperative associations (LWCAs), which are Maryland limited liability companies that elect to operate under worker-owned cooperative principles.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation and the Maryland Insurance Commissioner
stakeholders: Workers, small business owners, and entrepreneurs interested in worker-owned cooperative business models.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $278,400 in FY 2027 for one-time programming costs at the State Department of Assessments and Taxation to implement the new entity type. State revenues may see a minimal increase from filing fees associated with LWCA registrations. There is no anticipated material impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically tasks the Maryland Insurance Commissioner with enforcing Section 4A-12A-11, which regulates the calculation of workers' compensation insurance premiums for members of limited worker cooperative associations.

The bill amends several sections of the Tax - General Article to establish personal liability for taxes (admissions, motor fuel, income, and sales) for individuals managing limited worker cooperative associations. As the state's chief tax collector, this affects the Comptroller's enforcement and revenue collection duties.

The bill includes specific provisions regarding workers' compensation coverage for 'worker members' of these new associations, impacting the regulatory environment for workplace injury claims and mandatory insurance requirements.

The bill defines 'worker members' and clarifies that the formation of an LWCA does not create a presumption of employment for state law purposes, which is relevant to the Department's oversight of workforce development and labor standards.

As the agency responsible for stimulating private investment and supporting small businesses, the creation of a new legal entity for worker cooperatives provides an additional framework for economic development and entrepreneurship.
The fiscal note indicates a one-time general fund expenditure of $278,400 for programming costs, which falls under DBM's responsibility for overseeing state spending and the annual operating budget.
The OAG acts as the legal advisor to state agencies, including the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Comptroller, and will likely provide counsel on the implementation of this new act.
The bill establishes procedures for the judicial dissolution of limited worker cooperative associations and governance disputes, which impacts the administration of the state's court system.

bill_summary: This bill extends the noise abatement monitoring system pilot programs in Montgomery and Prince George's counties for an additional two years, moving the expiration date from 2026 to 2028. It also extends the associated reporting deadlines for the participating counties and establishes privacy protections for recorded images captured by these noise cameras, aligning them with the standards used for other automated enforcement systems like speed cameras.
responsible_party: Montgomery County and Prince George's County governments
stakeholders: Motorists and residents in Montgomery County and Prince George's County, as well as the Maryland District Court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill extends the potential for local revenue and expenditures related to noise abatement programs through FY 2028. State general fund revenues may increase minimally due to contested citations handled by the District Court. Montgomery County expects annual operating costs of approximately $99,400, while citation revenues are expected to be minimal for both counties because civil penalties are capped at $75.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the counties participating in the noise abatement monitoring pilot program to submit detailed performance and fiscal reports to the Governor by December 2027.
The fiscal note indicates that general fund revenues will increase if citations are contested in the District Court, impacting the state's revenue collection managed by the Comptroller.
The bill modifies the Public Information Act regarding the inspection of recorded images from noise abatement systems, requiring legal guidance from the OAG on privacy and data disclosure.
MDE is the state's primary regulatory agency for environmental health, including noise pollution, and was a consulted agency for the fiscal analysis of the pilot program.
The pilot program is authorized within the Transportation Article and affects the state's overall transportation and vehicle law policy, which is overseen by MDOT.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the central hub for public safety policy and grant administration; the extension of automated noise enforcement systems falls within its criminal justice policy interests.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Reservoir Augmentation Program within the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) to regulate the planned placement of highly treated reclaimed water into surface water reservoirs used as sources for drinking water. It requires a permit for such activities, sets stringent treatment standards, and creates a special fund for the program's operation and oversight. The bill also extends the existing Indirect Potable Reuse (IPR) Pilot Program from 2028 to 2030.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment
stakeholders: Public water system operators, local municipal governments, and Maryland residents using public drinking water systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $97,300 in FY 2026 to hire a contractual planner to establish the program, with costs continuing through FY 2028. Special fund revenues are projected to increase by $75,000 in FY 2030 from permit application fees. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, MDE is tasked with establishing and managing the Reservoir Augmentation Program, adopting necessary regulations, issuing permits, and overseeing the special fund created by the bill.

The bill establishes standards to protect public health during the reservoir augmentation process, and the fiscal note indicates MDH was a source of information during the analysis of the legislation.

MES operates water and wastewater treatment plants for various jurisdictions; as a fee-for-service entity, they may be engaged to design or operate reservoir augmentation facilities under the new permitting program.

The bill requires general fund expenditures for the creation of a new contractual position at MDE, which involves DBM's oversight of state personnel and budget allocation.
DNR manages state waters and natural resources; reservoir augmentation directly impacts surface water reservoirs and the broader aquatic ecosystem which falls under DNR’s conservation interests.

bill_summary: The bill updates the legal standards for compensating trustees and guardians of property. It also mandates that trustee compensation be split equally between trust income and principal while preserving existing commission rates for guardians of property.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Trustees, guardians of property, trust beneficiaries, and minors or disabled persons with guardianship estates.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may be affected by shifts in taxable income between trusts and trustees, but any impact is likely limited and difficult to estimate. State expenditures are not materially affected. Small businesses serving as trustees may see increased compensation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts judicial proceedings by establishing factors that courts must consider when determining the reasonableness of a trustee's compensation. It also governs the compensation of guardians of the property, who are often appointed and overseen by the judiciary.

The Register of Wills is responsible for overseeing the administrative probate of estates and protecting legal records related to those proceedings. bill_summary: This bill establishes a right to repair for powered wheelchairs, requiring manufacturers to make documentation, parts, embedded software, firmware, and tools available to independent repair providers and owners on fair and reasonable terms. The bill specifically covers components such as batteries, joysticks, wheel assemblies, and armrests while classifying violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.

stakeholders: Owners of powered wheelchairs, independent repair providers, and powered wheelchair manufacturers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not have a material impact on State or local finances. The Office of the Attorney General can handle enforcement with existing resources. Small businesses that repair powered wheelchairs may see a meaningful benefit due to increased access to repair resources, though authorized repair providers may face increased competition. Civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and $25,000 for repeat violations may apply under existing law.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes requirements under the Consumer Protection Act regarding the repair of powered wheelchairs. The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as the entity responsible for enforcing these provisions and investigating complaints.

As the state’s cross-disability policy leader, MDOD focuses on assistive technology and barrier-free environments. This legislation directly impacts the independence and mobility of Marylanders with physical disabilities by regulating the repair of powered wheelchairs, a core component of assistive technology mentioned in their mission.

A significant portion of older adults served by MDOA rely on powered wheelchairs for independence. The department’s role in advocating for and providing services to individuals with disabilities makes the availability of repair parts and documentation a pertinent issue for their constituency.

The fiscal note identifies a potential meaningful impact on small businesses that repair powered wheelchairs. As the primary agency for economic development and small business support, Commerce is relevant to the bill's impact on market competition between authorized and independent repair providers.

MDH administers the Medicaid program, which frequently funds powered wheelchairs for low-income residents. Changes to the repair landscape—specifically the availability of parts and documentation—may influence the maintenance costs and service life of equipment provided through state-funded healthcare programs.

The Governor’s Office is responsible for signing legislation and overseeing the operations of state departments, including those involved in consumer protection and disability services, to ensure statewide initiatives for economic opportunity and well-being are met.

It repeals the Interagency Committee on Aging Services, transferring its responsibilities to the Department, and requires the establishment of single points of entry within planning areas to provide information and services to older adults and their caregivers. The bill also transitions the terminology used in state law from seniors to older adults.

stakeholders: Older adults, caregivers, Area Agencies on Aging, non-profit organizations, assisted living facilities, and congregate housing providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill consolidates three existing programs which were allocated a total of $20.1 million in general funds in the fiscal 2026 budget. While the consolidation and transition planning are expected to be absorbed within existing resources, state general fund expenditures may increase starting in FY 2027 to the extent that the Department enters into new service agreements or contracts. Local government revenues and expenditures may increase if local agencies or Area Agencies on Aging enter into contracts with the State to provide the authorized services.

The legislation consolidates three of its existing programs (Senior Care, Senior Assisted Living Subsidy, and Congregate Housing Services Provider), repeals the Interagency Committee on Aging Services, and transfers those responsibilities directly to the Department. bill_summary: The bill repeals the existing criminal prohibition and associated misdemeanor penalty for an individual with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) who knowingly transfers or attempts to transfer the virus to another individual.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Individuals living with HIV, law enforcement, and the Maryland judicial system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local governmental finances or operations. While the bill repeals a specific misdemeanor, individuals may still be subject to prosecution for other criminal offenses such as reckless endangerment or assault. Historical data indicates very few charges and zero convictions for this specific offense in recent years.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the chief executive, the Governor is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation. This bill, named the Carlton R. Smith Act, represents a significant policy shift in public health and criminal law overseen by the Executive Branch.

The OAG serves as the legal advisor to state agencies, including the Department of Health, and manages criminal appeals. Repealing a criminal statute affects the state's legal framework and future appellate work.

This bill repeals a section of the Health-General Article, which the Department of Health is responsible for administering. MDH oversees infectious disease control and public health policy related to HIV/AIDS.
The AOC manages court operations and tracking of criminal charges. The fiscal note specifically includes data from the Judiciary regarding charges and convictions under the statute being repealed.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages the state's correctional system and community supervision. Repealing a criminal offense impacts potential incarcerations and the management of individuals under their custody.

As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the MSP is responsible for investigating crimes. Repealing this specific misdemeanor removes one legal basis for criminal charges related to the transfer of HIV.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD provides legal representation to indigent residents facing incarceration. This bill directly impacts the types of cases and charges they must defend in criminal and juvenile proceedings.
The GOCI serves as a liaison to diverse constituent groups, including LGBTQIA+ communities often impacted by HIV-related policy and advocacy efforts like the Carlton R. Smith Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and public safety policy, making the repeal of a criminal statute a direct interest to their policy work.

The Commission enforces anti-discrimination laws, including those related to physical disabilities. Repealing a law that criminalizes individuals based on their HIV status is relevant to their mission of preventing discrimination and promoting equal treatment.

bill_summary: This bill increases the fees for Maryland resident consolidated senior sport fishing licenses, angler’s licenses, and trout stamps for both residents and nonresidents. It also repeals the provision that previously exempted senior sport fishing license holders from the requirement to obtain a trout stamp to fish in designated trout areas.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR)
stakeholders: Maryland resident and nonresident anglers, senior citizens aged 65 and older, and businesses that sell fishing licenses or provide fishing guide services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues are projected to increase by $565,800 in FY 2025 and approximately $3.0 million annually starting in FY 2026. These revenues will be distributed to the Fisheries Management and Protection Fund and the Fisheries Research and Development Fund to support nontidal fishery management. General fund revenues will increase through FY 2028 due to interest earnings. There is no direct impact on State expenditures or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Natural Resources is the primary agency responsible for issuing the fishing licenses and trout stamps affected by the bill. The bill increases fees that flow directly into the Fisheries Management and Protection Fund and the Fisheries Research and Development Fund, which DNR uses to manage nontidal fisheries, hatcheries, and the Natural Resources Police.

The fiscal note specifically states that administrative expenditures from the Fisheries Management and Protection Fund, which this bill increases, support the costs of legal representation and advice provided by the Office of the Attorney General to the Department of Natural Resources.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees the formulation of the Governor’s annual operating budget and estimates state revenues. This bill addresses a projected fiscal imbalance in the Fisheries Management and Protection Fund, requiring DBM oversight of fund balances and administrative indirect cost methodologies.

As the state's independent tax collector and fiscal watchdog, the Comptroller is responsible for monitoring state revenues, including the special fund revenues generated by the increased license fees and general fund interest earnings discussed in the fiscal note.

The Treasurer’s Office is the custodian of the state’s financial assets and manages the investment of all public funds. The increase in special fund revenues and the associated interest earnings reported in the fiscal note directly fall under their management of the state's banking and investment services.

This is a departmental bill (requested by the Department of Natural Resources) that aligns with the Governor's authority to oversee state agencies and draft the annual budget. The Governor is responsible for signing the legislation and overseeing the fiscal health of the executive departments.

The Maryland Office of Tourism Development is responsible for promoting the state as a travel destination. Because fishing is a significant component of Maryland's heritage tourism and local economy, changes to nonresident license fees and the cost of recreational activities impact their marketing and economic development strategies.

bill_summary: This bill moves the deadline for filing a petition to form a new political party (or adding signatures to one) from the first Monday in August to the first Monday in July during presidential and gubernatorial election years. Additionally, it prohibits signatures that were part of a petition officially determined to be legally insufficient from being resubmitted with a subsequent petition.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Registered voters seeking to form new political parties, the Maryland State Board of Elections, and local boards of elections.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances. The State Board of Elections requested these changes to provide sufficient time for petition verification before producing ballots and updating voter communications for general elections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill was requested by the State Board of Elections and directly impacts their administrative processes for managing, verifying, and certifying petitions for the formation of new political parties, as well as the timelines for ballot production.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal advisor to the State Board of Elections and would be responsible for defending the state in litigation involving the disqualification of signatures or the denial of a political party's formation under the bill's new provisions.

The Governor's Office is responsible for signing election-related legislation and the bill specifically references the Governor's role in proclaiming special elections, which triggers specific petition filing timelines adjusted by this act.

Determinations made by the State Board of Elections regarding petition sufficiency are subject to judicial review; changes to filing deadlines and the eligibility of resubmitted signatures could lead to challenges heard within the state court system.

bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland's Building Energy Performance Standards (BEPS) by establishing an annual reporting fee, refining the definition of 'covered buildings' to exclude certain facilities like hospitals, and adding flexibility through new compliance credits and waivers. It requires the Maryland Department of the Environment to conduct a cost-benefit analysis of BEPS policy options and certify county-led performance programs.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE)
stakeholders: Owners of commercial and multifamily buildings (35,000+ sq ft), state and local government agencies, hospitals, manufacturing businesses, and energy auditors.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues increase by $690,000 in FY 2026 from reporting fees, while MDE administrative costs increase by approximately $1,033,837. A one-time general fund expenditure of $343,837 is required in FY 2026 to cover a funding gap. State and local government owners of covered buildings will incur costs for annual reporting fees.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, MDE is responsible for adopting regulations for building energy performance standards (BEPS), establishing Energy Use Intensity (EUI) targets, collecting fees, and conducting the required cost-benefit analysis of policy options.

DGS manages and maintains state-owned facilities. Since state-owned buildings 35,000 square feet or larger are 'covered buildings' under this bill, DGS is responsible for their compliance with energy standards and the payment of annual reporting fees.

The bill requires alternative compliance fees to be deposited into the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which is managed by MEA. MEA also coordinates clean energy incentives that building owners use to meet performance targets.

DBM oversees state agency expenditures and personnel. The fiscal note indicates significant budgetary impacts, including the need for general fund supplements and the allocation of funds for state agencies to pay building reporting fees.

The bill explicitly alters how health care facilities, hospitals, and nursing homes are treated under BEPS, including a specific exclusion for hospitals and special provisions for sterilization steam and backup power generation.
The Governor's Office provides executive oversight for MDE's regulatory rollout and is the recipient of the mandated BEPS policy analysis and recommendations due by December 2026.

The bill references manufacturing definitions within Labor's jurisdiction and involves requirements for energy auditors who may be licensed or regulated through the Department of Labor's professional boards.
Multifamily residential buildings are a primary category of 'covered buildings' subject to the standards and EUI targets established by this bill, which impacts DHCD's housing programs and oversight.
USM is a major owner of large-scale buildings that qualify as 'covered buildings.' The system will face significant operational and financial impacts to meet energy targets and pay annual fees.

As a state agency and major property owner with facilities exceeding the square footage threshold, Morgan State is directly impacted by the reporting fees and compliance requirements for its campus buildings.
The OAG provides legal counsel for the drafting and enforcement of MDE's regulations. The fiscal note identifies the need for an additional Assistant Attorney General to support the BEPS program.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates the state's sustainable growth and climate goals. This bill represents a core policy lever for the initiative's objective to reduce urban greenhouse gas emissions.
The Treasurer's Office serves as the custodian of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, which receives the alternative compliance pathway payments and fees generated by the bill.
The bill includes special provisions for 'critical infrastructure' and 'emergency facilities,' requiring coordination with MDEM's definitions and assessments of vital state networks.
Data centers are explicitly categorized as critical infrastructure in the bill, making DoIT's expertise relevant to how these facilities are handled under energy intensity exceptions.
The BPW may be required to review and approve significant state contracts for energy retrofits and modifications needed for state-owned buildings to comply with the new standards.

MDP provides technical assistance and policy guidance on land use and sustainable growth, which intersects with the long-term benchmarking and energy planning for covered buildings required by the bill.
The bill requires an analysis that must include recommendations on how to consider community colleges, which fall under MHEC's coordinating and regulatory oversight.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the June 30, 2025, termination date for the formula used to determine the maximum amount of user fees assessed by the Maryland Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) on hospitals and related institutions. By making the current assessment formula permanent, the HSCRC can continue to collect fees based on 0.1% of budgeted hospital revenue or the highest cap from the preceding five fiscal years to support its regulatory duties and the implementation of the Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development (AHEAD) Model.
responsible_party: Health Services Cost Review Commission
stakeholders: Maryland hospitals and related health institutions, the Maryland Department of Health, and Medicaid payers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Repealing the sunset provision is expected to increase HSCRC special fund revenues and expenditures by approximately $1,600,000 in FY 2026, rising to $4,800,000 by FY 2030. Additionally, total Medicaid expenditures are estimated to increase by $315,400 in FY 2026 and $963,300 in FY 2030 (comprising 40% general funds and 60% federal funds) due to higher hospital rates resulting from the fee assessment. Federal fund revenues will increase correspondingly to match federal expenditures. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The HSCRC is the primary agency affected, as the bill repeals the sunset on the formula used to determine its maximum user fee assessment, which is the commission's primary source of funding for its statutory duties and the implementation of the AHEAD model.

DBM is responsible for the state's central fiscal authority and must oversee the special fund revenue increases and general fund expenditure impacts on the Medicaid budget resulting from this legislation.

The Governor signed this departmental bill into law; it supports the state's agreement with the federal government to participate in the AHEAD Model, a key executive policy initiative for health equity and cost containment.
The OAG serves as the primary legal advisor for the HSCRC and the Department of Health, providing counsel on the regulatory and fee-collection processes addressed in the bill.

OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of executive agencies, including the HSCRC, to ensure that public funds and user fees are handled according to the repealed sunset provisions.

bill_summary: This bill makes several changes to the Maryland tax sale process to protect vulnerable homeowners and heirs. It requires local governments to withhold owner-occupied properties and those occupied by heirs of deceased owners from tax sale if delinquent taxes are less than $1,000. The bill limits the annual redemption interest rate for owner-occupied residential property to 10% and prohibits the inclusion of taxes and penalties accruing after the tax sale in the redemption payment for such properties. Additionally, it requires counties to establish registries for withholding properties from sale, expands the Homeowner Protection Program eligibility to include heirs, and extends notice requirements for tenants of properties in foreclosure.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT), specifically the State Tax Sale Ombudsman, and local county and municipal tax collectors
stakeholders: Owner-occupant homeowners, heirs of deceased property owners, low-income individuals, seniors, disabled residents, tenants of residential properties, local governments, and private tax sale certificate purchasers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State Annuity Bond Fund revenues are projected to decrease by up to $92,000 annually starting in FY 2026. Local government revenues may be significantly affected through delays or reductions, with an illustrative estimate of up to $1.1 million in annual revenue losses due to the 10% cap on redemption rates. Local expenditures may increase to cover administrative costs for implementing new property registries and differentiating between owner-occupied and non-owner-occupied properties in the tax sale process.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This is a departmental bill requested by the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD). The bill directly relates to their mission of neighborhood revitalization and housing stability by expanding protections for vulnerable homeowners and heirs to avoid foreclosure through the tax sale process, and it revises eligibility for the Homeowner Protection Program.

The bill alters the legal procedures for tax sale foreclosures, including changes to notice requirements for tenants and the State Tax Sale Ombudsman, timelines for filing complaints to foreclose the right of redemption, and the process for taking possession of property after a judgment.

The bill includes specific provisions allowing local governments to withhold dwellings from tax sale if they are owned or occupied by low-income individuals who are at least 65 years old, which directly impacts the department's advocacy and protection efforts for Maryland's older adults.

The bill contains provisions that allow for the withholding of property from tax sale for homeowners or heirs who are disabled, aligning with the department's mission to protect the rights and independence of individuals with disabilities.

The fiscal note indicates that the bill will delay or reduce revenues for the Annuity Bond Fund (State property tax revenues), which falls under DBM's oversight of state revenue estimation and fiscal accountability.

As the chief legal advisor for state agencies, the OAG will likely be involved in providing legal guidance on the revised tax sale foreclosure processes and the implementation of the new registry and notice requirements.

The bill involves significant changes to state tax law and executive agency programs (like HPP), which the Governor's Office oversees. The office is also responsible for the legislative review and approval of these reforms.

bill_summary: This bill increases the square footage threshold for State real property leases that can be entered into without competitive procurement from 2,500 square feet to 5,000 square feet. It also reduces the mandatory advertising period for State rental needs from 30 days to 20 days and requires that these needs be advertised on the Department of General Services website and the eMaryland Marketplace online procurement system.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of General Services
stakeholders: State agencies seeking to rent office space, commercial property owners and landlords, and the public in localities where the State is looking to lease property.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have no material impact on State or local finances. While the Department of General Services will adjust its procurement and advertising procedures for real property leases, these changes do not affect overall revenue or expenditure levels.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of General Services (DGS) is the primary agency responsible for managing the state's real estate leases and the eMaryland Marketplace procurement platform. This departmental bill directly alters DGS's procedures for advertising building needs and increases the square footage threshold for noncompetitive leasing, which DGS manages to improve efficiency.

The Board of Public Works is the highest administrative authority for state spending and is statutory required to review and approve state real estate leases. Changes to procurement thresholds and advertising timelines directly affect the flow of contracts and the regulatory framework that the Board oversees for state property management.

The Governor's Office is relevant because the Governor sits as one of the three members of the Board of Public Works, which is responsible for the final review and approval of the real estate leases impacted by the procedural changes in this bill.

The Comptroller of Maryland is a member of the Board of Public Works. In this capacity, the Comptroller acts as a fiscal watchdog and must review and approve significant state expenditures, including the building leases affected by the new thresholds and advertising requirements established by this bill.

The State Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works, which manages the state's procurement and capital improvements. The Treasurer's Office participates in the approval of the real property leases that are subject to the revised competitive requirements and expedited advertising periods defined in this legislation.

bill_summary: This emergency bill modifies the requirements for scheduling and conducting special elections to fill vacancies in a county council or the office of a county executive. It requires the date of a special election to be at least 90 days after the adoption of a resolution and prohibits scheduling it within 120 days of a regularly scheduled election. The bill also authorizes the State Administrator of Elections to oversee special elections when local and state laws conflict, removes the requirement for mailing specimen ballots in mail-in special elections, increases the timeframe for mailing ballots to voters to 30 days before the election, and allows the use of ballot drop boxes.
responsible_party: The State Administrator of Elections and local boards of elections
stakeholders: Registered voters in Maryland counties, local boards of elections, and county government officials including county councils and executives.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances. Local government finances may be indirectly impacted as the bill's scheduling restrictions may dictate whether special elections are held independently or concurrently with regular elections. For context, a countywide special primary election in Prince George’s County cost approximately 2100000 dollars in 2024, indicating the potential scale of local expenditures for independent special elections. The removal of specimen ballot requirements may provide some cost savings for mail-in special elections at the local level. Any change in the number of independent special elections held would impact local expenditures for staffing and ballot mailing and processing. No revenues are expected to be generated for either the State or local governments as a result of the bill's provisions. State Board of Elections indicates changes are necessary for administrative efficiency and to ensure voters have sufficient time to participate in special elections. Potential impacts are noted to be minimal for small businesses by the Department of Legislative Services and State Board of Elections because the changes relate to governmental administrative and legal protocols for elections rather than private sector activities or regulations affecting commerce and standard business operations in Maryland districts and counties during election cycles or periods of vacancy filling for county leadership roles. The emergency status ensures the bill takes effect immediately upon enactment to address current and upcoming election cycles without delay, potentially affecting special elections scheduled for later in the 2025 calendar year following the governor's approval date in late April of 2025 as indicated in the enacted legislation text provided in the source materials for this analysis of House Bill 75 and its fiscal impact note prepared by the Department of Legislative Services of the Maryland General Assembly for the 2025 legislative session cycle and the subsequent chaptering of the legislation into Maryland law following its passage and signature by the Governor Wes Moore on April 22nd, 2025. bill_summary: This bill establishes specific procedures and acceptable methods for an authorized fiduciary to provide notice or send documents when exercising decanting power under the Maryland Trust Decanting Act. It requires notice to be sent via methods likely to result in receipt, such as personal service, certified mail, or courier delivery, while also allowing for alternative methods like email or facsimile if the recipient agrees in writing.
responsible_party: Authorized fiduciaries (trustees or other fiduciaries with discretion to distribute trust property)
stakeholders: Authorized fiduciaries, qualified beneficiaries of trusts, and other persons entitled to notice under the Maryland Trust Decanting Act.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect State or local government finances. Small business impacts are expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills is responsible for overseeing the administrative probate of estates and protecting legal records related to the Estates and Trusts Article of the Maryland Code. This bill directly amends that article by establishing specific notice and transmittal requirements for trust decanting, a topic within their core domain of expertise and records management.

The Administrative Office of the Courts manages the infrastructure of the Maryland Judiciary. Because the Maryland Trust Decanting Act involves fiduciary powers that may be subject to judicial oversight or litigation, the AOC is relevant for ensuring that procedural changes regarding notice and document service are integrated into court education and administrative guidelines.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the state's chief legal advisor and was specifically consulted regarding the fiscal impact of this bill. Its Consumer Protection Division and general legal oversight units may have an interest in the fair notification practices established for authorized fiduciaries.

The Governor's Office is the principal executive agency responsible for signing legislation into law and overseeing the operation of state departments. The Governor officially signed this bill (Chapter 221) on April 22, 2025.

bill_summary: This bill establishes that each animal harmed in a violation of state animal cruelty laws is considered a separate offense and an individual victim for the purpose of the sentencing guidelines' stacking rule. It further specifies that a conviction for an animal-related crime may not merge with other convictions arising from the same act and that sentences may be served consecutively or concurrently. Additionally, the bill clarifies that certain animal cruelty prohibitions do not apply to legal hunting or fishing activities conducted using humane methods.
responsible_party: Judiciary and Maryland State Commission on Criminal Sentencing Policy
stakeholders: Individuals charged with or convicted of animal-related crimes, Maryland state and local courts, and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have a minimal fiscal impact. State and local revenues may increase slightly due to fines collected from animal cruelty convictions. State and local expenditures may also increase minimally if the new sentencing rules result in longer periods of incarceration or more individuals being committed to correctional facilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the sentencing guidelines 'stacking rule' and establishes that each animal harmed constitutes a separate offense, which judges and court staff must implement during sentencing proceedings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The prohibition on merging convictions and the requirement to treat each animal as a separate victim for sentencing significantly increases the potential penalties for defendants, directly impacting the agency’s defense strategies and caseload complexity.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's sentencing changes, including the non-merger of offenses and the ability to impose consecutive sentences, are expected to increase the length of stay and the population within state correctional facilities.

The bill creates specific exemptions for hunting and fishing activities that are conducted in compliance with Title 4 and Title 10 of the Natural Resources Article, which the department and its Natural Resources Police oversee.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Commission on Criminal Sentencing Policy (MSCCSP), which manages the sentencing guidelines and stacking rules explicitly modified by this bill, falls under this category of government bodies.
The bill establishes that animal cruelty laws do not apply to customary agricultural husbandry practices or food processing, both of which are regulated by the Maryland Department of Agriculture.

As a primary statewide law enforcement agency, the State Police investigate criminal acts including animal cruelty and will be responsible for charging violations under the new multi-offense framework.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's central hub for public safety policy, this office advises on criminal justice strategies and manages data/funding that would be affected by changes in animal cruelty sentencing and prosecution.
The OAG represents the state in criminal appeals and provides legal counsel to the agencies impacted by the implementation of new animal cruelty exemptions and sentencing rules.
The bill is expected to have a fiscal impact on state expenditures due to potentially longer incarceration periods, which DBM must account for in the executive budget.
As the office that signed the bill into law and oversees the executive agencies responsible for enforcement and corrections, it maintains high-level relevance to the implementation of the policy.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a population-based quota for Class A and Class D (off-sale) alcoholic beverages licenses in Anne Arundel County, limiting issuance to one license per 3,500 individuals in specified tax assessment districts. It also restricts the transfer of these licenses to locations within the same assessment district where they were originally issued or located as of July 1, 2025.

stakeholders: Current and prospective alcoholic beverages license holders in Anne Arundel County and residents of the county's tax assessment districts.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no effect on State finances. For Anne Arundel County, there is no impact on expenditures, and revenues are not expected to be affected as existing license renewals and transfers are permitted, even though five of the seven applicable districts currently exceed the population-to-license ratio.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor serves as the chief executive who signs legislation into law and oversees the operations of state boards. The Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners, which is the primary body responsible for implementing the license quotas and transfer restrictions in this bill, consists of members appointed by the Governor.

This office is responsible for recruiting and vetting candidates for state boards and commissions, including the Board of License Commissioners for Anne Arundel County, which is tasked with the direct enforcement of the population ratio quotas established by this bill.

The OAG serves as the legal advisor to state boards and commissions. As the Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners is a state-mandated regulatory body, the OAG would provide legal guidance on the implementation of the new population-based licensing restrictions and handle any related litigation.

The Comptroller is the state's chief fiscal officer and tax collector, responsible for monitoring business licenses and revenues related to alcoholic beverages. While the fiscal note identifies no immediate state fiscal impact, the agency maintains a role in the broader regulatory and fiscal oversight of the industry.

The bill establishes license quotas based on population estimates and specific tax assessment districts. The Department of Planning manages demographic and economic research and provides technical assistance to local governments regarding land use and community planning data.

As the state's economic development agency, Commerce monitors regulations that impact small business growth, competition, and the expansion of the retail sector, including the alcoholic beverages industry in specific counties.

The bill defines assessment districts based on a specific 'Official Map' titled 'Tax Assessment Districts, 2005.' The State Archives is the central depository for official government records and maps of permanent historical and legal value.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor for the State and its agencies, providing essential counsel on the legal implications of altering insurance pooling definitions and the powers of public entities.

The State Treasurer's Office manages the state's insurance and risk management programs; as the state's expert on public fund safeguarding and insurance, it has an interest in the framework for public entity insurance pools.
MDP coordinates sustainable growth and land use policy; Resilience Authorities support infrastructure that is critical to the long-term planning and sustainability of Maryland communities.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable growth and environmental stewardship efforts across MDE, DNR, and MDP, all of which intersect with the work of local Resilience Authorities.

Resilience infrastructure projects often involve protecting transportation networks (highways, bridges, and ports) from climate impacts, making MDOT a relevant stakeholder in the viability of Resilience Authorities.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies implementing resilience policies and is responsible for signing the bill into law to enable these authorities.

bill_summary: This bill makes significant revisions to the Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program, primarily by delaying its implementation. It pushes the start date for required contributions from July 1, 2025, to January 1, 2027, and delays benefit payments until a date between January 1, 2027, and January 3, 2028. The bill also introduces an 'anchor date' for benefit calculations, postpones the participation of self-employed individuals until the Department of Labor adopts specific regulations by July 1, 2028, and adjusts various reporting and administrative deadlines.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Maryland employees, employers with 15 or more employees, self-employed individuals, and community health service providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill delays the FAMLI Program's contribution and benefit start dates, resulting in a significant reduction in special fund activity. Special fund revenues decrease by approximately $1.3 billion annually in FY 2026 and FY 2027. Special fund expenditures for benefits decrease by up to $1.8 billion in FY 2027 and $946.7 million in FY 2028. In FY 2026, general fund expenditures increase by $37.3 million for administrative costs (offset by other savings for a net $22.5 million increase) due to the lack of available special fund revenue. Local governments will also realize expenditure savings from delayed employer contributions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for administering the Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program. The bill directly revises the department's duties, including the creation of regulations for self-employed enrollment, the setting of contribution rates, and the timeline for benefit payments.

The bill explicitly mandates that the Maryland Department of Health reimburse community providers for their share of FAMLI contributions. The delay in the program causes a significant multi-million dollar reduction in health-related expenditures for fiscal years 2026 and 2027.

The bill effectuates a major shift in the state budget, moving approximately $37.3 million from general funds to replace special fund administrative costs. DBM is responsible for the state personnel system and the fiscal oversight impacted by these billion-dollar fund delays.

The bill directly alters the statutory timeline for the Board of Public Works to perform its duty of determining whether economic conditions allow for the indexing of maximum weekly benefits, delaying this responsibility from 2026 to 2028.

The Comptroller manages the state’s central payroll and will be responsible for implementing FAMLI contribution deductions for over 100,000 state employees. The delay in the program significantly impacts the Comptroller's implementation timeline and revenue tracking duties.

As the custodian of the state's financial assets, the Treasurer manages the investment of the FAMLI Fund. The billion-dollar shifts in revenues and the program's revised fiscal structure directly impact the management of these public funds.

The bill is a departmental initiative from the executive branch that delays a landmark statewide policy. The Governor is responsible for signing the legislation and overseeing the agencies implementing these large-scale administrative revisions.

The OAG serves as the legal advisor to the Department of Labor and will be responsible for providing counsel on the drafting of new regulations for self-employed individuals and ensuring compliance with revised statutory definitions like 'anchor date.'

The bill references the Insurance Article regarding employer insurance pools and restricts the Department of Labor from requiring certain pools to escrow funds. The delay also affects the regulatory environment for private FAMLI insurance plans.

The OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal and performance audits of state agencies. The management of the revised FAMLI fund and the Department of Labor's adherence to new administrative deadlines will be a subject of future audits.

The delay in the FAMLI Program impacts the procurement and development timeline of the complex IT infrastructure required for processing claims and managing employer accounts, which falls under DoIT's strategic oversight.

stakeholders: Food-insecure Maryland residents, Maryland farmers, nonprofit farmers markets, and nonprofit organizations involved in food access programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State finances, as it primarily redirects the authorized uses of the existing Maryland Farms and Families Fund. The Governor is responsible for drafting the annual budget, which must include the mandated appropriation for the Fund. Additionally, the Governor oversees all state departments, including Agriculture, and is responsible for signing the bill into law.
The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to account for the Maryland Farms and Families Fund, which is established as a special, nonlapsing fund.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the Maryland Farms and Families Fund separately from other state funds.

DHS is the primary provider of SNAP benefits in Maryland. The bill's program aims to double the purchasing power of SNAP benefits for food-insecure residents, directly impacting the population served by DHS.

The Maryland Department of Health provides public health services and coordinates local health efforts. The bill's program impacts WIC benefit recipients by doubling their purchasing power at farmers markets.

bill_summary: This bill regulates automatic renewal offers for consumer contracts, requiring sellers to clearly disclose renewal terms, provide accessible and easy-to-use cancellation methods, and send advance notices before a renewal or a free trial (lasting more than 14 days) takes effect. Violations are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, though the bill does not authorize a private right of action for damages.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
stakeholders: Maryland consumers and businesses that offer automatic renewal subscriptions or purchasing agreements.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no material impact on State or local finances or operations. The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division can implement the bill using existing resources. While existing civil penalty provisions under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act apply to violations, they are not expected to significantly affect state revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Attorney General (OAG), primarily through its Consumer Protection Division, is the lead agency responsible for enforcing the Maryland Consumer Protection Act (MCPA). This bill classifies violations of the new automatic renewal regulations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the MCPA, granting the OAG direct oversight and enforcement authority over sellers failing to provide required notices or easy cancellation mechanisms.

The Governor's Office serves as the principal executive agency and is responsible for signing legislation into law and overseeing the operations of state departments. Governor Wes Moore signed this bill, which impacts executive enforcement policy and coordinates with other state agencies excluded from the bill's provisions.

The bill explicitly excludes businesses and individuals with contract renewal practices already subject to regulations, rules, or procedures established by the Maryland Insurance Administration (MIA). This maintains the MIA's independent regulatory jurisdiction over insurance-related subscriptions and policies.

The bill explicitly excludes services regulated by the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC). This provision ensures that utility companies and other entities under PSC oversight continue to follow commission-specific regulations regarding service agreements and renewals rather than being subject to this broader consumer protection statute.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) provides an impartial forum for Maryland residents to challenge agency decisions. Since enforcement of this bill falls under the MCPA, administrative proceedings initiated by the OAG (such as cease and desist orders) would be adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges within the OAH.
