bill_summary: This bill requires State or State-aided or controlled entities to include a provision in maintenance contracts requiring prime contractors to purchase janitorial products from Blind Industries and Services of Maryland (BISM) if the products are packaged or repackaged by BISM and are available.
responsible_party: State procurement units, including the Department of Budget and Management and the Department of General Services
stakeholders: Blind Industries and Services of Maryland (BISM), prime contractors for State maintenance contracts, and small business janitorial suppliers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to have a direct effect on State or local finances, though it may have a minimal operational effect on State procurement units. There is a potential meaningful impact on small businesses that provide janitorial supplies, as they may have fewer opportunities to participate as subcontractors or suppliers on State maintenance contracts.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of General Services is the state's central procurement unit for facilities and commodities. It is responsible for managing state building maintenance and will be the primary agency tasked with enforcing this procurement preference in janitorial and housekeeping contracts.

DBM serves as a central procurement authority and personnel management agency. The bill impacts state procurement policy and fiscal procedures, which DBM helps oversee and estimate for the Governor's budget.

The Board of Public Works approves major state procurement contracts and ensures compliance with statutory preferences. This bill modifies the criteria for janitorial product procurement that the Board must oversee in maintenance contracts.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees all state departments and signed this legislation into law. The office is responsible for the general administration of executive procurement policies.

The Comptroller sits on the Board of Public Works and acts as the state's fiscal watchdog. This agency is involved in approving the state contracts that are now subject to the expanded BISM packaging preference.
The Treasurer sits on the Board of Public Works and manages the state's financial assets. The office participates in the oversight of state procurement and policy decisions impacted by this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note indicates a potential meaningful impact on small businesses that provide janitorial supplies, as they may lose sub-contracting opportunities to BISM. This office monitors such procurement impacts on the small business community.

MDOT is a primary procurement unit that manages extensive infrastructure and facilities requiring significant janitorial and maintenance services. It must ensure its contractors comply with the updated BISM preference.

As a major state entity with its own procurement authority and numerous campus facilities, USM must implement the requirement to procure BISM-packaged janitorial products in its maintenance contracts.

Morgan State University is a primary procurement unit with independent management of its urban campus. It must adhere to the bill's requirements for janitorial product sourcing in its facility contracts.
As a state agency and public college with independent procurement functions, it is required to follow state preferences for janitorial products within its maintenance agreements.
The bill directly supports Blind Industries and Services of Maryland, which aligns with the department's mission to promote the independence and employment of individuals with disabilities.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and reviews procurement contracts for legal sufficiency. It will assist agencies in updating contract language to include the new packaging and repackaging preferences.

responsible_party: Maryland Historical Trust
stakeholders: Local governments, genealogical and historical organizations, descendant communities, religious and local cemetery operators, and state historic preservation agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $42,200 in FY 2026 only to hire one contractual staff position at the Maryland Historical Trust to support the workgroup. There is no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Maryland Historical Trust (MHT), which is part of the Department of Planning, to provide primary staff support for the workgroup. Additionally, the Director of MHT is a designated member of the workgroup.

The bill includes the Executive Director of the Maryland Office of Cemetery Oversight (within the Department of Labor) as a workgroup member and grants the Secretary of Labor the authority to appoint several other members representing local and religious cemeteries and genealogical organizations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill explicitly establishes a new Workgroup (the Maryland Inventory of Cemeteries and Burial Sites Workgroup) to study specific policy issues and report recommendations, fitting the definition of this designation.
The Maryland State Archivist, or their designee, is a mandatory member of the workgroup and provides historical and record-keeping expertise necessary for creating a cemetery inventory.

The Chief of the Office of Cultural Resources in the Maryland Department of Transportation is a mandatory member of the workgroup, reflecting the agency's interest in historical site preservation during infrastructure planning.

The fiscal note indicates that the Office of the Attorney General will handle legal research and analysis associated with the workgroup’s responsibilities, such as reviewing statutory definitions of burial sites.

The bill has a fiscal impact of $42,200 in general fund expenditures for FY 2026 to hire a contractual position to staff the workgroup, which falls under DBM's oversight of state personnel and budgeting.
The workgroup is required to submit its final report of findings and recommendations to the Governor by December 1, 2025.
The workgroup includes the Chair of the Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture, an entity for which GOCI provides administrative oversight and outreach coordination.

The Department of Commerce supports small businesses; this bill impacts the service offerings and operational limitations of small retail businesses such as barbershops and beauty salons.

The Secretary of State certifies official state documents and manages administrative functions related to the certification of laws passed by the General Assembly.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits a person from keeping a rooster movement-constrained through the use of an enclosure or tether starting January 1, 2027, subject to specific exceptions for commercial producers, schools, animal shelters, animal welfare organizations, and members of certain youth programs. It establishes civil penalties for violations and grants enforcement authority to State and local law enforcement as well as local animal control authorities.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Agriculture, State and local law enforcement officers, and local animal control authorities
stakeholders: Rooster owners, commercial poultry producers, public and nonpublic schools, government-operated animal shelters, animal welfare organizations, and members of 4-H or Future Farmers of America programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to have a minimal impact on State revenues due to the collection of civil penalties. State enforcement can be handled with existing resources. Local government expenditures for animal control and law enforcement may increase minimally in some jurisdictions, but local revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill identifies the 'Department' (Agriculture) as the primary authority responsible for adopting regulations, granting authorizations for keeping roosters beyond the specified limits, and coordinating enforcement efforts with local animal control and law enforcement.
The Governor's Office oversees all state departments involved in the bill's implementation, and the Governor is responsible for signing the legislation into law.
The Maryland State Police are explicitly authorized to enforce the new restrictions on keeping roosters and may issue civil warnings and penalties for violations.

The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Department of Agriculture for the development of required regulations and represent the state in any legal challenges regarding the enforcement of animal treatment laws.
The Judiciary, through the Administrative Office of the Courts, manages the processing of civil citations and the collection of fines associated with the new civil offenses established by the bill.
The OAH serves as the venue for individuals to appeal civil penalties or administrative decisions made by the Department of Agriculture regarding rooster keeping permits and violations.
The Natural Resources Police (NRP) within DNR are state law enforcement officers who may encounter and enforce these poultry-related violations, particularly in rural and agricultural areas.

Public and nonpublic schools that receive state funds are specifically exempted from the bill's restrictions, which may require the department to provide guidance to educational institutions regarding their status.
DBM oversees the fiscal notes and potential (though minimal) increases in general fund revenues generated by the new civil penalties.

bill_summary: This bill updates the regulatory framework for the practice of chiropractic in Maryland by revising Board membership appointment processes, education requirements, and examination standards. It replaces the previous extern license with a temporary license, defines preceptorships for students, and expands the Board's disciplinary authority to include unannounced office inspections for infection control violations and mandated health examinations for practitioners suspected of posing a risk of harm to the public.
responsible_party: State Board of Chiropractic Examiners
stakeholders: Licensed chiropractors, chiropractic license applicants, chiropractic students, and patients receiving chiropractic care in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures are expected to be handled within existing budgeted resources, with minimal changes to board special fund spending. State general fund revenues may increase minimally due to the expansion of grounds for civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. There is no impact on local government revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent agency of the State Board of Chiropractic Examiners, the Maryland Department of Health is responsible for the board's administrative and regulatory oversight, which is significantly updated by this bill regarding licensure, office inspections, and disciplinary procedures.

The Office of Administrative Hearings conducts the formal, trial-like proceedings for contested disciplinary cases involving healthcare professionals; the bill expands the grounds for discipline and board authority, likely increasing or altering the scope of these hearings.

The Governor is responsible for appointing the chiropractor and consumer members of the State Board of Chiropractic Examiners; the bill specifically modifies the nomination requirements and the size of the candidate list submitted to the Governor.

This office vets and recruits candidates for gubernatorial appointments to over 600 boards, including the State Board of Chiropractic Examiners, which is directly impacted by the bill's changes to board membership rules.

The Office of the Attorney General provides primary legal counsel and representation to state agencies and health occupation boards, including managing civil appeals related to the Maryland Chiropractic Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department maintains the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS), which is required by the bill to perform the state and national criminal history records checks mandated for temporary license applicants.

The bill allows for civil penalties of up to $5,000 to be imposed in lieu of or in addition to license suspension; these penalties are deposited into the State General Fund, which the Comptroller oversees as the state's revenue collector.

The bill references board activities authorized 'in accordance with the State budget,' and as the state's central fiscal authority, DBM oversees the budget and personnel management for the Department of Health and its boards.

The bill replaces board-specific approval of chiropractic schools with a requirement for programs to be accredited by specific national or foreign entities recognized by the U.S. Department of Education, impacting the oversight of these programs of study.

As the state's coordinating board for postsecondary education, this agency is affected by the bill's shift from board-approved 'schools' to accredited 'chiropractic programs of study' and the alignment of these programs with workforce needs.

It reduces the annual license fee for veterans' organizations from $400 to $300, permits the Board of License Commissioners to offer application and administrative fee discounts, and allows these organizations to sell alcohol on Sundays without the need for a separate Sunday license.
responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Veterans' organizations in Anne Arundel County and their members
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. Anne Arundel County revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $2,400 annually beginning in fiscal 2026. This estimate is based on the expectation that eight existing Class C license holders will convert to the veterans' organization license, which has a lower fee and includes Sunday sales. There is no impact on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically benefits veterans' organizations by reducing annual alcoholic beverage license fees and expanding Sunday operating hours in Anne Arundel County. As the state's primary advocate and resource hub for veterans and their organizations, this agency would be interested in the fiscal and operational relief provided to these community groups.

As the primary legal advisor for the State and the agency responsible for representing nearly all state agencies, the OAG may provide counsel on the interpretation of the amended Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article and the legal definitions of eligible veterans' organizations.

The Comptroller serves as the state’s chief financial officer and has general oversight of revenue collection and business licensing frameworks. While the bill primarily impacts local county revenues, the Comptroller monitors the state's broader licensing environment and fiscal health.

bill_summary: This bill establishes privacy protections for recorded images and data produced by automated enforcement systems, such as speed, red-light, and school bus cameras. It restricts access to these images without a warrant, subpoena, or court order except for specific traffic or law enforcement purposes, prohibits the use of biometric or facial recognition technology, and mandates the immediate destruction of images that do not show a violation. Additionally, it requires agencies to adopt security and audit procedures and sets limits on how long evidence of a violation may be retained.
responsible_party: State police department, State Highway Administration, local police departments, and local agencies operating automated enforcement programs
stakeholders: Maryland motorists, pedestrians, State and local law enforcement agencies, and the State Highway Administration
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates operational and potential administrative costs for State and local law enforcement agencies to manage record destruction, audit processes, and program procedures. Agencies that knowingly violate the bill's privacy provisions are subject to a fine of up to $1,000 for each violation. The Judiciary is expected to handle any increase in warrant or subpoena requests with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Chief Judge of the District Court, whose administrative functions are supported by the AOC, to adopt procedures for the issuance of citations, trials, and collection of civil penalties for all automated enforcement programs. The Judiciary also handles the increased demand for warrants, subpoenas, and court orders required to access recorded images.

The bill explicitly defines the State Highway Administration as an 'agency' responsible for implementing and operating automated enforcement programs, such as work zone speed control systems. It must comply with new privacy, storage, and destruction requirements for recorded images.

The Maryland State Police is specifically named in the bill as an 'agency' that operates automated enforcement systems. It will be directly responsible for following new protocols regarding data access, warrants, and the mandatory immediate destruction of non-violating images.

MDOT is the parent department for several agencies (SHA, MTA, MVA) that either operate automated enforcement systems or manage the vehicle data necessary to process the resulting citations. It oversees the multi-modal network where these systems are deployed.

The bill amends Section 4-321 of the General Provisions Article (the Public Information Act), which is overseen by the OAG. The agency provides legal counsel on PIA denials and will be responsible for advising State agencies on compliance with the new privacy and warrant requirements.

The bill specifically covers bus lane monitoring systems, which are operated by the MTA to record images of motor vehicles committing violations. The MTA must adhere to the new standards for image processing and disposal.

The MVA manages vehicle registrations and driver records which are essential for identifying owners and processing citations generated by automated systems. It also handles specialty plates and regulatory compliance related to highway safety.

School bus monitoring cameras are a major component of the bill's automated enforcement categories. MCSS coordinates school safety grants and technical assistance, often involving these monitoring technologies.

MSDE oversees the safety of K-12 students, including the regulation of school bus operations. The bill impacts how school bus monitoring cameras—authorized to catch vehicles passing stopped buses—manage and store recorded images.

The bill establishes strict new retention and destruction schedules for recorded images (ranging from immediate destruction to a maximum of 5 years). The State Archives is the central authority for setting records management and disposal policies for State agencies.

The fiscal note indicates potential administrative and operational costs for State agencies to implement new audit processes, storage software, and destruction procedures. DBM oversees the fiscal accountability and budgets for these departments.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a judge to consider whether a military protection order (MPO) has been issued against a respondent when determining whether to grant a temporary peace order or temporary protective order. Additionally, it requires law enforcement officers to notify the relevant military law enforcement agency if they have probable cause to believe a service member has violated an MPO that is recorded in the FBI's National Crime Information Center database.

stakeholders: Service members in the U.S. uniformed services and National Guard, individuals seeking peace or protective orders (petitioners), judges, and law enforcement officers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $99,900 in FY 2026 for one-time programming costs for the Judiciary. There is no effect on State revenues. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Administrative Office of the Courts is the primary entity impacted by the bill's fiscal requirements. The fiscal note identifies $99,900 in general fund expenditures for one-time programming costs to update judicial systems to incorporate Military Protection Orders (MPOs) into temporary peace and protective order proceedings. Additionally, judges within the court system must now consider MPOs as a factor in these hearings.

As the head of the Maryland Military Department, the Adjutant General oversees the Maryland National Guard. The bill's definition of 'military protection order' specifically includes orders issued by commanding officers within the Maryland National Guard, making the agency a primary stakeholder in how these orders interact with civilian court systems.

The bill explicitly incorporates military protection orders issued by the Maryland National Guard into the state's legal framework for peace and protective orders. The notification requirements for law enforcement officers directly impact how violations involving Guard members are communicated back to military authorities.

As the primary statewide law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are directly impacted by the new mandate requiring officers to notify the entering agency when a service member is believed to have violated a military protection order found in the NCIC database.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically mentions the Executive Director of the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy in its definitions. GOCPP serves as the hub for public safety policy and manages victim services programs, making it relevant to the implementation of cross-jurisdictional protection order protocols.

This agency acts as an advocate for Maryland's military community. The bill directly affects the safety and legal status of service members and their families by allowing state judges to consider military-specific protection orders in civilian cases.

The Department of Human Services handles child and adult protective services. Since protective orders are a core tool for the safety of the populations they serve, the inclusion of military protection orders in the judicial decision-making process is relevant to their welfare mission.

The Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) Police, a unit of MDOT, are law enforcement officers who will be subject to the bill's new requirement to notify specific agencies when a service member violates a military protection order.

The Natural Resources Police (NRP) are state law enforcement officers. Under the bill, NRP officers must follow new protocols to notify the issuing agency if they have probable cause to believe a service member is violating an MPO.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal advisor for state agencies and the Judiciary. They would likely provide legal guidance on the enforcement of the new notification requirements and the standards for judicial consideration of MPOs.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for overseeing state expenditures. It will be involved in the allocation and management of the $99,900 identified in the fiscal note for the Judiciary's IT upgrades.

As the chief executive office responsible for enforcing state laws and drafting the annual budget, the Governor's Office oversees the Comptroller's operations and signed this legislation into law. The fiscal impact on the general fund affects the state’s broader financial management.

Synopsis: Authorizing food establishments that are businesses that conduct agritourism, Class 4 limited wineries, or Class 8 farm breweries to comply with the requirement to provide a convenient lavatory by providing a portable chemical toilet that is supplied with approved hand drying devices, kept in a sanitary condition, is properly ventilated, and is placed at least 25 feet from a well.

bill_summary: This bill allows specific food establishments, including agritourism businesses, Class 4 limited wineries, and Class 8 farm breweries, to meet the legal requirement for providing a convenient lavatory by using a portable chemical toilet, provided the toilet is sanitary, properly ventilated, supplied with hand-washing materials, and placed at least 25 feet from a well.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and Local Health Departments
stakeholders: Agritourism businesses, Class 4 limited wineries, and Class 8 farm breweries
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no effect on State or local revenues. The Maryland Department of Health and local health departments can update regulations and perform necessary inspections using existing budgeted resources. Small businesses may experience a positive fiscal impact through reduced upfront construction costs for permanent lavatory facilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Health - General Article, specifically Section 21-325, which the Department of Health is responsible for enforcing regarding the sanitation and licensing of food establishments. The agency will be required to update regulations and provide guidance to local health departments.

The bill directly impacts agritourism businesses, farm breweries, and wineries. The Department of Agriculture is responsible for promoting and protecting the economic viability of these agricultural and resource-based industries.

The bill specifies that portable chemical toilets must be placed at least 25 feet from a well. The MDE is responsible for protecting state water resources and regulating the safety of public drinking water systems and general environmental sanitation.

The bill affects wineries, farm breweries, and agritourism businesses, which are key sectors for private investment and job creation. The Department of Commerce supports the expansion of these small businesses through economic development initiatives.

This agency advocates for the 18 rural counties of Maryland where agritourism, farm breweries, and wineries are primarily located. The bill addresses unique infrastructure challenges faced by these rural businesses.

Agritourism, wineries, and farm breweries are primary drivers of heritage and agricultural tourism. This agency promotes Maryland as a premier travel destination and supports the growth of these specific visitor-facing industries.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note indicates the bill has a meaningful impact on small businesses by reducing the upfront capital costs required to build permanent lavatory facilities for new agritourism or farm-based beverage operations.

The bill defines eligibility for the portable toilet exemption based on the definition of 'agritourism' found in the Land Use Article, which is a policy area overseen and coordinated by the Department of Planning.

responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections
stakeholders: Members and candidates of the Baltimore County Republican and Democratic party central committees, and voters in Baltimore County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no direct impact on State or local government finances. Both State and Baltimore County revenues and expenditures are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for managing and supervising elections in Maryland, including the certification of ballots. Since central committee members are elected during primary elections, the board must implement the changes to the committee structures and ballot compositions mandated by this bill.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the chief legal advisor for the State and its agencies. It would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the State Board of Elections regarding the implementation of changes to the Election Law Article and defending the state in any potential legal challenges related to the alteration of political party central committee structures.

The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly. This bill was signed into law by the Governor, and the office oversees the executive branch's compliance with these new legislative requirements.

The Maryland State Archives maintains the Maryland Manual On-Line, which serves as the official record of the state's government structure, including descriptions of political party central committees. The Archives would be responsible for updating historical and current records to reflect the altered membership numbers.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a venue beer, wine, and liquor license in Dorchester County for nonprofit or for-profit retail businesses that host events such as weddings, banquets, and meetings. To qualify, a venue must be at least 2,000 square feet, accommodate at least 100 people, and have adequate bathroom facilities. The license allows the sale of alcohol for on-premises consumption only when food is also provided. The bill also permits the issuance of this license to establishments within 300 feet of a school or place of worship, provided written consent is obtained from the affected institutions.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Dorchester County
stakeholders: Nonprofit and for-profit retail businesses in Dorchester County hosting events; event organizers and attendees; schools and places of worship in Dorchester County.
fiscal_impact_summary: Dorchester County revenues will increase starting in fiscal 2026 from the collection of $1,500 annual license fees. The exact increase depends on the number of licenses issued. The county can manage enforcement with existing resources. There is no impact on Maryland State finances. Small businesses eligible for the license may experience a meaningful fiscal benefit.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly, including this bill which creates a new alcoholic beverages license class in Dorchester County.

The Comptroller is the state's tax collector and fiscal watchdog; the establishment of new licenses for the sale of beer, wine, and liquor will generate state revenue through sales and use taxes on alcoholic beverages.
The OAG serves as the primary legal advisor for the State and its agencies, providing expert counsel on the interpretation and enforcement of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

The bill specifically addresses the issuance of alcoholic beverages licenses within 300 feet of public and nonpublic schools, which falls under MSDE's broad oversight of the K-12 education environment.

The Maryland Department of Health directs the activities of local health departments, which are responsible for inspecting food service facilities and ensuring adequate sanitation/bathroom facilities at event venues as required by the bill.

The Maryland State Police oversees the State Fire Marshal’s Office, which is responsible for enforcing fire safety and occupancy standards for public assembly venues such as those defined in the bill (minimum 2,000 square feet/100 individuals).

The MCSS is dedicated to fostering safe and inclusive learning environments; the provision allowing liquor licenses within 300 feet of schools with consent relates to their mission of monitoring the safety and emotional well-being of school communities.

Synopsis: Requiring the State Board of Pharmacy to send renewal notices to licensees, permit holders, and registrants by electronic means, rather than by first-class mail, unless the licensee, permit holder, or registrant requests to receive the renewal notice by first-class mail.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits

bill_summary: This bill requires the State Board of Pharmacy to send license, permit, and registration renewal notices to recipients via electronic means (email) instead of first-class mail. Licensees and permit holders may still request to receive their notices via first-class mail. If an electronic notice is returned as undeliverable, the Board is required to send a follow-up notice via first-class mail.
responsible_party: State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Licensed pharmacists, pharmacy permit holders, registered pharmacy technicians, wholesale distributor permit holders, and registered pharmacy interns.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the State Board of Pharmacy are estimated to decrease by approximately $14,500 annually beginning in FY 2026 due to reduced printing and postage costs associated with electronic notifications. There is no impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees the operations of state departments like the Maryland Department of Health. The Governor is also responsible for signing the legislation into law.

The bill has a direct fiscal impact on state special fund expenditures, which DBM oversees as the central fiscal authority. The fiscal note indicates an annual decrease in expenditures of approximately $14,500 due to reduced printing and mailing costs.

The State Board of Pharmacy is a unit within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly alters the administrative requirements for the Board, shifting its primary notification method for thousands of licensees and permit holders to electronic means.

The bill mandates a shift to electronic renewal notices, which may require coordination with DoIT regarding cybersecurity standards, email infrastructure, and digital government service modernization.

OLA conducts fiscal and compliance audits of executive branch agencies. They will be responsible for verifying that the State Board of Pharmacy is complying with the new statutory notification requirements during future audit cycles.

The OAG acts as the legal advisor for the State Board of Pharmacy and the Department of Health. They may provide counsel on the legal requirements for valid electronic notification and handling undeliverable communications.

responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Dorchester County
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders in Dorchester County, including restaurants, bars, and retailers, and the Dorchester County local government.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. Locally, Dorchester County revenues are projected to increase by at least $10,250 annually starting in fiscal 2026 due to the modified license fees. This revenue estimate is based on the 66 active licenses that would be subject to fee increases. There is no impact on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly. This bill was signed into law by Governor Wes Moore as Chapter 832 of the 2025 Laws of Maryland.

The Office of the Attorney General acts as the primary legal advisor to the Governor and the General Assembly, reviewing legislation for legal sufficiency and providing counsel on the implementation of state laws.

The bill increases and alters licensing fees for various alcoholic beverage licenses, which the fiscal note indicates will have a potential meaningful impact on small businesses such as restaurants, bars, and retailers—a key constituency that the Department of Commerce supports through business development and economic monitoring.

The Comptroller serves as the state's fiscal watchdog and independent tax collector. While these fees are local to Dorchester County, the Comptroller oversees state-level revenue reporting and the broader fiscal health related to alcohol commerce and taxation in Maryland.

The Maryland State Archives is the central depository for government records of permanent value and maintains the Maryland Manual On-Line, which documents changes to state and local laws and the powers of local boards.

bill_summary: The bill requires the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development to notify the State Department of Assessments and Taxation when a commercial property developed under federal law has been awarded a low-income housing tax credit. responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Developers and owners of low-income housing properties, low-income tenants, and state and local tax assessment officials.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax controversies, the Maryland Tax Court is responsible for resolving appeals regarding property assessments. The bill's specific valuation requirements for LIHTC properties will govern the Court's legal determinations in relevant cases.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including DHCD, and would be responsible for advising on the implementation of the new reporting requirements and defending the state's valuation methods in court.

bill_summary: The Raymono A. Russell Act requires Maryland public library branches to install and maintain automated external defibrillators (AEDs) in prominent, accessible areas starting January 1, 2026. Libraries must comply with the Public Access Automated External Defibrillator Program, and the bill provides civil immunity for libraries and individuals who use or fail to use an AED in good faith during cardiac emergencies. bill_summary: This bill authorizes Anne Arundel County and its municipalities to grant a personal property tax credit to supermarkets that undergo new construction or substantial renovation and are located within a designated food desert retail incentive area. The local governments are responsible for defining these areas and establishing eligibility criteria for the credit.
responsible_party: The governing body of Anne Arundel County or a municipal corporation in Anne Arundel County
stakeholders: Supermarkets and residents in food desert retail incentive areas in Anne Arundel County
fiscal_impact_summary: State effect is none. Anne Arundel County and municipal personal property tax revenues will decrease starting in FY 2026 to the extent the tax credit is granted. The decrease depends on the number of qualifying supermarkets, their personal property value, and the credit amount provided. Local expenditures are not significantly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill authorizes tax incentives for supermarkets in food desert retail incentive areas, which directly supports the department's mission of neighborhood revitalization and stimulating local economic growth in underserved commercial areas.

Addressing food deserts and food insecurity is a primary policy goal for this office in its efforts to combat childhood poverty and improve the well-being of families through coordinated state support networks.

As the state's primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce is interested in business attraction and expansion initiatives, such as these tax credits intended to encourage private investment in retail infrastructure.

The elimination of food deserts is a significant public health strategy aimed at improving nutrition and reducing health disparities, aligning with the department's responsibility to protect and promote community health.

The department coordinates sustainable growth and community vitality; incentivizing essential services like supermarkets in underserved urban or municipal areas is a core component of local planning and smart growth strategies.

This agency focuses on data-driven solutions to reduce childhood poverty and increase economic mobility, themes that are directly addressed by improving retail food access and economic incentives in disadvantaged areas.
The Governor's Office oversees statewide initiatives for economic opportunity and child well-being and is responsible for signing the legislation that enables these local property tax credits.

bill_summary: This bill alters the collective bargaining process for uniformed fire employees of the BWI Airport Fire and Rescue Department by establishing a binding arbitration process if an impasse is reached in negotiations. It requires the parties to reach an agreement by September 30th and defines the timeline for arbitration, though arbitrator decisions regarding wages remain subject to state budget limitations.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation and the Department of Budget and Management
stakeholders: Uniformed fire employees of the BWI Airport Fire and Rescue Department and State executive branch agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures from the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) and potentially the general fund may increase starting in FY 2026. Costs include shared arbitrator fees (estimated at $375 to $1,125 per hour) and potential increases in personnel and related expenditures resulting from binding arbitration awards beginning in FY 2027. There is no impact on state revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: BWI Airport Fire and Rescue Department employees are directly under the Maryland Aviation Administration's jurisdiction. The bill's changes to collective bargaining and binding arbitration processes directly impact MAA's personnel management and operational budget.

As the parent department of the Maryland Aviation Administration, MDOT oversees the Transportation Trust Fund, which funds BWI Fire and Rescue personnel. The bill potentially increases TTF expenditures and requires MDOT participation in new arbitration processes.

DBM serves as the state’s central personnel and fiscal authority. The fiscal note indicates DBM is involved in labor negotiations alongside MDOT and may incur additional costs related to the arbitration process and personnel workload.

The PERB oversees collective bargaining for the state's public workforce. The bill creates a specific arbitration process that may impact the board’s jurisdiction and operational workload regarding BWI Fire and Rescue employees.

Under Section 3-501 of the State Personnel and Pensions Article, the Governor is responsible for designating the representative to participate in collective bargaining on behalf of the state. The bill specifically alters the timeline and methodology for these executive negotiations.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including MDOT and DBM. They would likely be involved in reviewing the legality of binding arbitration outcomes and representing the state in any legal disputes arising from the collective bargaining process.

OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits of executive agencies. To the extent the bill increases state expenditures through binding arbitration, OLA would be responsible for auditing the use of funds in future cycles to ensure compliance with the resulting Memoranda of Understanding.

bill_summary: The Educational Equality for Service Members Act expands the legal definitions of "service member" and "veteran" across several Maryland Code articles to include all individuals serving in the uniformed services, specifically incorporating the Commissioned Corps of the Public Health Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. By aligning State definitions with federal standards, the bill ensures these service members and their families are eligible for state-provided benefits and privileges, including expedited educator and EMS licensure, nonresident tuition exemptions at public colleges, and eligibility for specific state scholarship programs.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education, Maryland Higher Education Commission, and Maryland public institutions of higher education
stakeholders: Active duty service members and veterans of the uniformed services (including the Armed Forces, Public Health Service, and NOAA), their spouses and dependent children, public school students, and professional licensure applicants.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures and scholarship fund expenditures are expected to increase starting in FY 2026 to accommodate additional recipients of the Edward T. and Mary A. Conroy Memorial Scholarship, with an estimated cost of $9,200 per award annually. Public institutions of higher education may experience a minimal loss in tuition revenue due to expanded nonresident tuition exemptions. Local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Department of Education by requiring expedited educator licensure for active service members and eligible veterans, altering public school enrollment rules for military dependents, and overseeing the Purple Star Schools Program for military-connected students.

MHEC is a primary agency for this bill as it oversees the Edward T. and Mary A. Conroy Memorial Scholarship Program and the Douglas J.J. Peters Veterans of the Afghanistan and Iraq Conflicts Scholarship, both of which have their eligibility criteria expanded by this legislation.

The bill updates the core definitions of 'veteran', 'service member', and 'uniformed services' in Section 9-901 of the State Government Article, which is the enabling statute for this department and its advocacy programs.

The bill affects the Maryland Disability Employment Tax Credit, which the Department of Labor administers in consultation with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. It also impacts workforce development and apprenticeship programs that may serve the broader category of 'uniformed services' members.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The legislation explicitly requires the EMS Board to credit training and experience gained by members of the 'uniformed services' (including PHS and NOAA) toward EMS licensure and certification requirements.

The bill mandates that member universities provide nonresident tuition exemptions to a broader group of active service members and veterans and requires the establishment of veterans resource centers on campuses.

As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State is impacted by the bill's requirements to grant nonresident tuition exemptions to the expanded categories of service members and their families.
The college must comply with the bill's provisions regarding nonresident tuition exemptions for active service members and veterans, as well as maintaining advisory services for student veterans.

The bill amends provisions related to the Maryland Senator Edward J. Kasemeyer Prepaid College Trust, specifically concerning the time allowed for beneficiaries in active duty to exercise their benefits.
The Treasurer's Office now oversees Maryland 529, and the bill impacts the administration of the Prepaid College Trust and related student financial assistance provisions.
The Comptroller is responsible for processing the Maryland Disability Employment Tax Credit, which is affected by the bill's change in definitions for qualified disabled veterans.

The bill expands the definitions of active duty and service members to include all uniformed services and reserve components, which directly involves the National Guard units commanded by the Adjutant General.
The bill affects the Maryland Technology Internship Program, which involves students and is mentioned as being within the scope of altered definitions in the fiscal note.
DBM oversees the state personnel system and the fiscal impact on entitlement programs like scholarships and tuition waivers that are expanded under this bill.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Small Business Development Financing Authority to provide loan guarantees for small businesses using various financial instruments, including irrevocable letters of credit, official treasurer's checks, and funds on deposit in escrow accounts. These instruments can be used to guarantee up to 80% of long-term loans made by financial institutions for purposes such as working capital, debt refinancing, equipment acquisition, and real property improvements.
responsible_party: Maryland Small Business Development Financing Authority
stakeholders: Small businesses, particularly those owned by socially and economically disadvantaged persons, and private financial institutions.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the Maryland Small Business Development Financing Authority are not expected to be materially affected because activity under the Long-term Guaranty Program is historically limited. State revenues are not affected, and there is no material impact on local government finances. The impact on small businesses is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce administers the Maryland Small Business Development Financing Authority (MSBDFA). This bill directly modifies the operational capabilities of MSBDFA by authorizing additional financial instruments, such as letters of credit and depository accounts, to be used for its Small Business Guaranty Fund.

The bill explicitly authorizes the use of 'official treasurer's checks' and depository accounts as forms of guaranty. As the agency responsible for managing the state's banking services and public funds, the Treasurer's Office is directly involved in the administrative and fiscal oversight of these specific instruments.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSBDFA programs are primarily intended to support small and socially or economically disadvantaged businesses. This office serves as a key liaison and advocate, connecting entrepreneurs from these groups to state-funded economic opportunities like the Small Business Guaranty Fund.

The Governor's Office provides executive oversight for the Department of Commerce and drives statewide policy initiatives aimed at increasing economic mobility and opportunity. This legislation aligns with the administration's goals for small business support and economic development.

The bill's inclusion of 'any other legal instrument' as a permissible form of guaranty requires legal review and guidance from the Office of the Attorney General to ensure that such instruments are legally sound and appropriately protect the state's interests.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Board of Nursing to hold discussions with the nursing boards of Delaware, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia to pursue reciprocity agreements for advanced practice nursing licensure and specialty certification. The goal is to increase access to qualified advanced practice registered nurses, enhance licensure portability, and improve telehealth access.
responsible_party: State Board of Nursing
stakeholders: Advanced Practice Registered Nurses (APRNs), the State Board of Nursing, nursing licensing boards in neighboring states/DC, and Maryland healthcare patients.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's requirements can likely be handled with existing budgeted resources. If additional staff is required, State Board of Nursing special fund expenditures may increase by approximately $90,000 for a contractual health policy analyst. Special fund revenues may experience a minimal decrease if out-of-state APRNs are no longer required to pay Maryland-specific licensure and certification fees due to new reciprocity agreements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Nursing is a regulatory unit within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly mandates the Board to negotiate reciprocity agreements and provides oversight for advanced practice nursing licensure and specialty certification.

The bill explicitly aims to facilitate telehealth access, a key area of policy and standard-setting for the MHCC. Additionally, the fiscal note indicates that the MHCC assesses fees on APRN licenses, which would be impacted by shifts in licensure volume.

The OAG serves as the legal advisor to the State Board of Nursing. It would be responsible for reviewing, drafting, and approving the legal framework of reciprocity agreements with Delaware, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia.

The fiscal note identifies a potential need for additional contractual staff (such as a health policy analyst) to handle the negotiations and reporting requirements, which involves DBM's personnel and budgetary oversight.
As the regulator of the state's insurance market, the MIA is impacted by changes in APRN licensure and telehealth portability, which affect provider networks and coverage for Maryland residents.

The OLA conducts fiscal and performance audits of the Department of Health and its boards. It would eventually be responsible for auditing the Board of Nursing's implementation and management of these new reciprocity agreements.

The Governor’s Office oversees all executive agencies, including the Board of Nursing and the Department of Health. The Governor is responsible for signing the legislation and receiving reports on the progress of interstate negotiations.

OAH serves as the neutral forum for challenging state agency decisions. If the Board of Nursing denies licensure or reciprocity under the new agreements, those disputes could be adjudicated by OAH Administrative Law Judges.

Advanced practice nursing requires graduate-level education. Reciprocity changes affect the labor market for nursing graduates and potentially influence the alignment of academic programs with regional workforce needs.

Instead of being required to mail physical notices to all employers, the Comptroller is authorized to provide these notices via electronic means or by mail.
responsible_party: Maryland Comptroller's Office
stakeholders: Employers in the State of Maryland and Maryland employees eligible for the Earned Income Tax Credit.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures are expected to decrease by more than $100,000 annually starting in fiscal 2026 due to reduced mailing costs, which currently total approximately $140,000. In fiscal 2026, these savings will likely be offset by one-time programming costs for the Comptroller's new integrated tax system. The bill has no impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for administering the Earned Income Tax Credit and is explicitly mandated by the bill to prepare and provide the notices to employers. The bill directly alters their administrative process and is expected to result in annual fiscal savings for the agency.

The Maryland State Innovation Team is specifically tasked with addressing childhood poverty and increasing economic mobility, with an explicit focus on expanding access to the Earned Income Tax Credit. The bill's aim to improve employer notification methods directly aligns with these initiatives.

The bill has a notable fiscal impact on the State's general fund expenditures, resulting in an estimated net savings of over $100,000 annually. As the central fiscal authority, the Department of Budget and Management is responsible for overseeing state expenditures and revenue estimations.

The bill shifts a government notification process from manual mail to electronic means to increase efficiency and reach more employers. This alignment with government modernization and efficiency falls within the agency's mission to enhance the responsiveness and performance of state government.

bill_summary: This bill clarifies the calculation of the local earned income tax credit by defining the 'applicable county income tax rate.' For counties with marginal income tax rates, the credit is calculated using the lowest marginal rate. For counties with flat rates that vary by income or filing status, the rate used is the one specific to the taxpayer's income level and status. The bill effectively codifies existing practices used by the Comptroller for counties that have already adopted tiered or bracketed tax structures.
responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Maryland taxpayers eligible for the local earned income tax credit and Maryland county governments, particularly those utilizing bracket-based or tiered income tax rates.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is considered clarifying in nature and is not expected to have a direct impact on State or local revenues as it aligns the law with current administrative practices. The Comptroller's Office can implement the changes using existing budgeted resources, and there is no impact on local expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for collecting state and local revenues and administering tax credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit. This bill was introduced at the request of the Comptroller's Office to clarify the calculation of local credits.

The Innovation Team's summary explicitly mentions a focus on reducing childhood poverty and economic mobility, specifically highlighting their work in expanding access to the Earned Income Tax Credit.

As the chief executive agency, the Governor's Office oversees state departments like the Comptroller and signed this legislation into law. The bill aligns with the Governor's stated priorities regarding economic opportunity and poverty reduction.
DBM is responsible for estimating state revenues and oversees the executive branch's fiscal accountability. Changes to tax credit calculations impact revenue forecasting and fiscal policy.
The OAG serves as the legal advisor to the Comptroller and the General Assembly, ensuring that changes to the Tax - General Article are legally sound and defensible.
DHS provides essential economic assistance to low-income residents. The Earned Income Tax Credit is a critical component of the financial safety net for the population served by DHS.

The GOC leads the state's efforts to eliminate childhood poverty. Clarifying and maintaining the local EITC is a direct tool in their mission to support low-income families and improve economic mobility.

bill_summary: This bill expands the criminal prohibition against willfully destroying or removing items from a cemetery to include landscaping or any other part of the cemetery grounds. It also extends the statute of limitations for prosecutions related to destroying funerary objects and cemetery elements to three years from the date local authorities knew or should have known of the violation.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and State's Attorneys' Association
stakeholders: Cemetery owners, cemetery managers, heirs and descendants of the deceased, and local law enforcement.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect Maryland State or local government finances or operations. While it expands the scope of a misdemeanor and extends the statute of limitations, there were no individuals sentenced under these specific crimes in circuit courts during fiscal 2024.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article to increase the statute of limitations for misdemeanor prosecutions related to cemetery destruction from one year to three years after the violation is discovered. This directly impacts court caseloads, judicial scheduling, and administrative procedures for the Maryland Judiciary.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands the scope of criminal acts prohibited in cemeteries and extends the time frame during which individuals can be prosecuted. This will require the OPD to provide legal representation and develop defense strategies for indigent clients facing these updated criminal charges.

The agency manages the Cemetery and Memorials Program, which includes five state veterans' cemeteries. The bill's expanded protections for cemetery grounds and funerary objects, as well as the extended statute of limitations for vandalism, directly impact the protection and management of these state facilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill impacts criminal penalties for misdemeanor violations, including potential imprisonment and fines. The fiscal note specifically mentions that the Division of Parole and Probation manages supervision cases for violations of the cemetery destruction statutes affected by this bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's central hub for public safety policy, GOCPP is responsible for advising the Governor on criminal justice strategies. This bill involves policy changes regarding criminal statutes, statutes of limitations, and property crimes within cemeteries.

The MSP is the primary statewide law enforcement agency responsible for investigating criminal violations. The bill updates the Criminal Law Article regarding the destruction of funerary objects and cemetery elements, which falls under their investigative jurisdiction.

The Maryland Department of Planning oversees the Maryland Historical Trust, which is responsible for preserving the state’s archaeological and historic sites, including historic cemeteries. The bill's emphasis on protecting funerary objects and cemetery landscaping aligns with their historic preservation mission.

The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor for the state and manages criminal appeals. Since this bill amends the Criminal Law and Courts and Judicial Proceedings Articles, the OAG would be involved in legal interpretations and subsequent appellate litigation related to these changes.

The Commission manages an 850-acre archaeological park that includes historic 17th-century burial sites. The bill's specific protections for funerary objects and grounds of a cemetery are highly relevant to their mandate to protect archaeological and historical records.

DNR manages over 500,000 acres of public lands, which include state parks and forests that occasionally contain historic or abandoned burial sites. The expanded criminal protections for cemetery elements apply to these public lands.

Vandalism and the destruction of property are offenses that can involve juvenile populations. As the agency responsible for the supervision and rehabilitation of youth in the justice system, DJS may manage cases related to the newly defined or expanded prohibitions in this bill.

The Archives preserve records of permanent historical value, including land and vital records that define historic cemetery boundaries and burial sites. While they do not enforce the law, their records are essential for identifying the objects and grounds protected by this bill.

Rural areas often contain smaller, family-owned, or historic cemeteries that are more vulnerable to neglect or vandalism. The Council advocates for the preservation of rural cultural assets, making this bill relevant to their community sustainability and advocacy efforts.

Synopsis: Clarifying which telephone calls the Comptroller of the State may record and monitor for training, quality control, and employee safety purposes; and providing that the Comptroller may monitor and record calls to the Comptroller's call centers only.

bill_summary: This bill clarifies the authority of the Maryland Comptroller to record and monitor incoming telephone calls by updating terminology from automated call distribution systems to Comptroller's call centers to reflect modern technology. The bill maintains existing privacy protections, including notice requirements to callers, a prohibition on recording direct individual lines, and restrictions on how long recordings may be retained and how they can be used in legal proceedings.
responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Maryland taxpayers, callers to the Comptroller's Office, and employees of the Comptroller's call centers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state or local fiscal impact. According to the fiscal note, the bill does not materially affect the operations or finances of the Comptroller's Office.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly regulates the Comptroller’s call center operations, including the authority to record and monitor calls, retention policies for those recordings, and limitations on how that data may be used.

The OAG serves as the primary legal advisor to the Comptroller and handles civil appeals, making it responsible for interpreting and defending the Comptroller’s call-recording and evidence-usage policies.

The bill explicitly prohibits the use of recorded call information in criminal or civil proceedings against Maryland taxpayers, which has a direct impact on the admissibility of evidence in cases before the Tax Court.

The OLA conducts compliance audits of state agencies and would be responsible for ensuring the Comptroller adheres to the statutory 60-day retention limit and other recording protocols established by this bill.

As the agency responsible for the strategic direction of state IT infrastructure, DoIT is relevant to the bill’s modernization of call center terminology and the underlying technology used by the Comptroller.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch operations and signs or vetoes legislation affecting the administrative powers of state departments like the Comptroller’s Office.
The bill’s restrictions on information usage in civil and criminal proceedings intersect with the judicial administration's oversight of court records and evidentiary standards.

The bill allows exceptions for recorded calls to be used in criminal proceedings if a threat is made against a state employee or property, potentially involving MSP in investigations and evidence handling.
DGS manages state-owned facilities and the Maryland Capitol Police; it is relevant because the bill addresses personal and imminent threats against state property and employees.

bill_summary: This bill expands the existing sales and use tax exemption for cannabis transactions to include sales between licensed cannabis businesses and registered cannabis nurseries. It ensures that business-to-business transactions involving registered nurseries are treated the same as those between licensed cannabis businesses, which are already exempt from the 9% sales and use tax.
responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Licensed cannabis businesses and registered cannabis nurseries
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no expected impact on State or local finances. The bill is clarifying in nature, as business-to-business transactions were intended to be exempt, and the Fiscal and Policy Note for the legislation that originally established cannabis nurseries did not assume any sales and use tax revenues from these transactions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the state's chief tax collector. This bill was introduced at the request of the Comptroller to clarify and expand the sales and use tax exemption for cannabis transactions to include registered nurseries, which the agency is responsible for administering.

The MCA is the primary regulatory body for the cannabis industry in Maryland. The bill specifically relates to the tax status of businesses licensed and nurseries registered by the MCA under Title 36 of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor oversees the operations of the Maryland Cannabis Administration and is responsible for signing or vetoing the legislation. The bill originated as a departmental request within the executive branch.

DBM oversees the state's fiscal policy and revenue estimates. While the fiscal note indicates no significant impact, the agency monitors changes to the sales and use tax code for long-term fiscal planning.

stakeholders: Justice-involved individuals currently serving or recently released (within 2 years) from a prison sentence of 6 months to 10 years, excluding those who committed crimes while holding elected office.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy

The Governor serves as the chief executive who signed the bill into law and oversees the implementing departments.
The OAG acts as the primary legal advisor for the agencies implementing the program and would likely be involved in drafting regulations.
This court adjudicates tax controversies and would handle appeals related to tax assessments or program eligibility determinations.
DBM estimates state revenues and manages the fiscal impact of tax-related legislation, including the forgone interest and penalties under this program.

bill_summary: This bill expands the Janet L. Hoffman Loan Assistance Repayment Program (LARP) to include veterinary practitioners and veterinary technicians. To be eligible, these individuals must have received a degree from an accredited veterinary college or university and provided veterinary services as an employee in Maryland for at least five years, or as a volunteer for at least 100 hours per year for at least three years at specified animal shelters.
responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission (Office of Student Financial Assistance)
stakeholders: Veterinary practitioners, veterinary technicians, and animal shelters owned by local governments or specific non-profit organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not mandate additional spending for the program, as new applicants may be placed on a waiting list if current appropriations (approximately $4.1 million for fiscal 2026) are insufficient. However, the Maryland Higher Education Commission will incur a one-time cost of approximately $8,000 in fiscal 2026 for software upgrades. Each individual award averages about $5,800. There is no impact on local government revenues or expenditures, though local animal shelters may benefit from increased staffing or volunteers.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Higher Education Commission, through its Office of Student Financial Assistance, is the primary implementing agency for the Janet L. Hoffman Loan Assistance Repayment Program. This bill directly expands the program's eligibility to include veterinary practitioners and technicians, requiring the Commission to manage new applications, update its processing systems (MDCAPS), and conduct publicity.

The bill defines eligibility for the loan program based on service at shelters that are recipients of the Maryland Spay and Neuter Grants Program, which is administered by the Department of Agriculture. MDA also provided critical data for the fiscal note regarding the veterinary industry and grant recipients.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees the state's annual budget and the appropriation of funds for the Janet L. Hoffman LARP. DBM is responsible for managing the program's funding levels, which the fiscal note indicates may be impacted by the increased number of eligible applicants.

The University System of Maryland oversees the public institutions that graduate many of the veterinary practitioners and technicians who would benefit from this program. USM is also tasked with workforce development in high-demand fields, making the incentives provided by this bill relevant to their strategic goals.

As the principal executive agency, the Governor's Office is responsible for signing the legislation and overseeing the agencies (specifically MHEC and MDA) tasked with implementing the expanded eligibility for the loan repayment program.

The Department of Health has a role within the Janet L. Hoffman LARP statute to determine 'high-need geographic areas' for other medical and counseling professions. While they do not lead the veterinary expansion, they are involved in the overall regulatory framework of the program.

The designation of special event areas for alcohol consumption may impact state-owned multi-modal transportation networks or require coordination for municipal events near state infrastructure.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) and the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to jointly conduct an annual assessment of the school health and wellness personnel workforce in Maryland. The assessment includes identifying student-to-provider ratios, vacancy rates, and strategies for improving recruitment and retention. The bill also adds a school nurse member to the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland State Department of Education
stakeholders: School health and wellness personnel (including counselors, dental hygienists, occupational therapists, physical therapists, school nurses, school psychologists, and social workers), local school systems, local health departments, and Maryland students.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no fiscal effect in FY 2026. Starting in FY 2027, State general fund expenditures increase by $61,700 to hire one part-time health policy analyst at the Maryland Department of Health to coordinate data collection and annual reporting. Annual expenditures are projected to be between $57,700 and $62,900 through FY 2030. Local school systems and health departments can manage the data reporting requirements using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Maryland Department of Health to jointly conduct an annual assessment of the school health and wellness personnel workforce, submit a report to the General Assembly, and publish the findings. Additionally, the Secretary of Health is an ex-officio member of the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers, and the fiscal note identifies a direct expenditure increase for a new analyst position within the department to handle these tasks.

The State Department of Education is jointly responsible for conducting the annual workforce assessment and reporting the findings. The State Superintendent of Schools also serves as an ex-officio member of the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers, and the department will be required to coordinate with local school systems to gather data on vacancy rates and recruitment strategies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies the composition and voting membership of the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers, an advisory body that fits the description of this functional designation within the executive branch.

As a centralized hub for school safety coordination that bridges the gap between students and mental health professionals, this agency is a key stakeholder in the assessment of school health and wellness personnel, including counselors and psychologists.

The Governor is responsible for appointing the 16 voting members of the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers, and the bill specifically adds a new member (a school nurse) to this group.

This office is responsible for vetting candidates to serve on the state’s boards and commissions. It will manage the recruitment and vetting process for the new school nurse member added to the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers.

The fiscal note identifies a fiscal impact requiring the creation of a new part-time position at the Maryland Department of Health. DBM acts as the central personnel and budget authority responsible for approving and managing such positions and fund allocations.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is a named ex-officio member of the Maryland Council on Advancement of School–Based Health Centers, the composition of which is altered by the bill.

The GOC leads a 'whole-of-government' approach to children's well-being, including access to mental health and healthcare services, which aligns with the bill’s goals of assessing the school-based health and wellness workforce.

The workforce assessment specifically includes personnel categories such as occupational therapists, physical therapists, and speech-language pathologists, who are critical to providing services to students with disabilities—a cross-disability policy area overseen by this department.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits a person from knowingly and willfully dismembering, destroying, removing, burying, or disposing of human remains with the intent to conceal a crime. It also prohibits aiding or abetting another person in these acts, classifying the offense as a felony punishable by up to five years in prison.
responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals involved in criminal activities related to human remains, law enforcement agencies, the Maryland judicial system, and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund incarceration expenditures may increase minimally due to the bill's five-year felony penalty provision. The bill is not expected to materially affect local finances or operations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill creates a new felony offense punishable by up to five years in prison, which will directly impact incarceration expenditures and the population levels of state correctional and community supervision facilities.

The judicial branch will be responsible for adjudicating and managing the trial processes for cases arising from the new criminal offense of dismembering or burying human remains with the intent to conceal a crime.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is tasked with providing legal representation for indigent residents facing potential loss of liberty, and this new felony statute will lead to an increased caseload for its attorneys.

As the primary statewide law enforcement authority, the Maryland State Police will investigate instances of remains disposal and destruction intended to facilitate the concealment of criminal activity.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy

The OAG manages all criminal appeals in state courts and provides legal counsel to the executive branch regarding the implementation and enforcement of the Criminal Law Article.
The agency maintains vital death records and regulates legal methods of body disposal, which provides the regulatory context for existing laws mentioned in the bill's analysis.
The Governor's Office signed the legislation into law and oversees the principal executive agencies responsible for criminal investigations, corrections, and judicial coordination.
